name: microkernel-plugin
context: The Microkernel pattern (also called Plugin Architecture) structures an application as a minimal core with extensible plugins. The core handles essential operations while plugins extend functionality without modifying core code. This pattern excels when different customers or users need different feature combinations, enabling customization without redeployment.
benefits: Extensibility: Add new features without modifying core
Customization: Different customers enable different plugins
Isolation: Plugin failures don't crash the core system
Independent deployment: Plugins can be developed/deployed separately
Fault tolerance: Core remains stable even if plugins malfunction
Testability: Plugins can be tested in isolation with mocked core
Agility: Module boundaries and APIs are stable, enabling quick response to change
tradeoffs: Complex development: Requires thoughtful design and contract governance
Low scalability: Product-based implementations are generally smaller, single deployment
Core stability requirement: Core must remain minimal; frequent changes defeat the purpose
Plugin interdependencies: Creates coupling that breaks isolation benefits
Contract versioning overhead: APIs must be stable or backwards compatible
Governance complexity: Must manage plugin lifecycle, compatibility, and discovery
use_cases: Building a customizable product with optional features
Need to add new features without modifying core code
Multiple customers with different feature needs
IDE, browser, or tool requiring extensions
Rules engine, workflow system, or processing pipeline
E-commerce platform with swappable payment processors
avoid_when: Small, simple applications where extension points cost not justified
Need true network isolation and fault boundaries
component_types: Core System (Microkernel): Minimal, stable kernel providing essential operations: plugin registry, lifecycle management, core contracts/APIs
Plugin Registry: Tracks installed plugins, their capabilities, and how to load them
Lifecycle Manager: Handles plugin initialization, startup order, shutdown, and potential hot-swapping
Event Bus: Optional message-passing mechanism for plugin-to-plugin or plugin-to-core communication
Extension Points (Contracts): Well-defined contracts/interfaces that plugins implement
Plugins (Extensions): Independent modules that implement specific features
anti_patterns: Distributed monolith (plugins requiring distributed deployment but tight coupling)
Shared database between plugins (creates data-level coupling)
Plugin interdependencies (Plugin A depends on Plugin B)
Core accumulating responsibilities (violates minimal core principle)
Unversioned contracts (breaking changes without deprecation path)
Cross-plugin direct calls (increases coupling beyond core)
design_principles: Keep the core minimal: Core should be < 500 LOC ideally; any logic that could be plugin-specific should be in a plugin
Plugins must be independent: No cross-plugin dependencies; communicate via core events/APIs
Use event-driven communication: Via core event bus rather than direct plugin calls
Versioned contracts: APIs must be stable or backwards compatible; check compatibility before registration
Add fitness functions: Forbid cross-plugin imports, pin allowed dependencies, fail build on violations
Explicit plugin metadata: Declare version, dependencies, compatibility in manifest
best_practices: Start with stable core identification: Invest time upfront to find truly stable, rarely-changing aspects of your system
Design extension points carefully: Well-defined contracts are critical; they must be stable and well-documented
Implement plugin isolation: Each plugin should be independently testable with mocked core dependencies
Use explicit configuration: YAML/JSON configuration for plugin discovery with validation and detailed error logging
Add lifecycle hooks: Implement init() and shutdown() methods; consider hot-swapping support
Enforce namespace isolation: Prefix plugin names by category to avoid naming conflicts
Plan governance from day one: Discovery/activation should validate signatures, permissions, compatibility with kill-switches
Standardize observability: Logs, metrics, and traces should include plugin identifiers and versions
Consider security sandboxing: Put authorization at the core; sandbox plugin I/O and secrets; audit plugin loading
Cache capability lookups: Measure p95/p99 on core-plugin calls; design retries and kill-switches per plugin
